title: MVP Development Cost: What Affects Your Budget?
excerpt: MVP development cost depends on the work included in your first release and the services you need afterward. Learn how to compare estimates and use the budget worksheet to track payments, responsibilities, and costs that still need confirmation.
body:
> **At a Glance**
>
> MVP development cost depends on the work included in your first release and the services you need afterward. Learn how to compare estimates and use the budget worksheet to track payments, responsibilities, and costs that still need confirmation.

MVP development cost can be difficult to judge when each estimate describes a different version of your idea. One developer may include design and launch, while another expects you to arrange them. Before comparing totals, you need to understand the work and assumptions behind each number.

That gives you a more useful budgeting question: what will it take to put this first version into use, support the trial, and respond to what you learn?

## How Much Does It Cost to Build an MVP?

There is no standard price for an MVP. A minimum viable product is an early usable version built to test an important assumption with real users. That purpose can require very different amounts of work depending on the product.

Published estimates show how widely the assumptions vary. In its 2026 guide, EnactOn describes builds from about $5,000 to $100,000 or more, spanning lean products through complex enterprise work. MetaProject gives a $50,000–$150,000 range for its senior-team framing, with a core workflow, real accounts, and production basics.

Those figures belong to the publishers' stated approaches and scopes. Neither tells you what your particular product should cost. To get a useful estimate, a developer needs to assess the task, existing assets, constraints, and unresolved questions.

The resulting build estimate is one part of your MVP budget. You also need to allow for services and work you pay for separately, including the period when customers begin using the product.

## What Affects MVP Development Cost?

A feature name leaves much of the work unspecified. Understanding the decisions beneath it helps you ask why an item has been estimated a certain way and which change could make the first release more affordable.

### Scope, Platforms, and User Roles

The scope needs to describe what users can complete, where they can complete it, and who has permission to do what. Each of these decisions can add behavior that must be designed, built, and checked.

A customer account and a staff account may show similar information but allow different actions. Staff might correct a record, while customers can only view it. Those rules still need implementation even if they add no new screens.

Platform requirements matter too. Tell the developer whether users need a browser, a mobile app, offline access, or particular devices. Ask what each option adds to the work. Choose the supported context around actual user needs before requesting a price for every platform.

### Design and Existing Work

The design allowance depends on what is already decided and what still needs to be worked out. A supplied visual design can help, but the developer must understand whether it covers the full task and its less obvious states.

For example, the interface may need to explain an empty account, an invalid entry, a failed save, or a restricted action. Ask whether the estimate includes designing those states, adapting layouts to smaller screens, and reviewing the result with you.

Existing code also needs assessment before anyone promises savings. The developer should check whether it can be run, changed, and released, and identify which parts are suitable to retain. A working demo alone does not establish how much usable implementation is already there.

### Integrations and Existing Data

Connecting another system can involve more than sending information between two applications. Access, data formats, limits, and failure behavior all affect the work. Comparing alternative approaches makes those differences easier to question in an estimate.

Consider an imaginary wholesale order portal. A version that sends a stock request to staff can leave confirmation to a person. A version that confirms stock automatically needs access to the inventory system and rules for unavailable or outdated information. The two versions make different promises to the customer, so ask which promise the estimate covers.

Importing existing records creates another set of questions. Are fields consistent? Are there duplicates? Who decides which record is correct? Ask whether preparation and checking of imported data are included, and who will supply the information needed to resolve problems.

### Technical Unknowns and Required Checks

Some work cannot be estimated confidently until a specific question has been investigated. The budget should make that uncertainty visible and identify what evidence would help the developer narrow the estimate.

An unfamiliar system connection might need a small test before the main build. Agree what that investigation will establish, what it will deliver, and when you will decide whether to continue. A price for the investigation does not automatically cover the implementation that follows.

Testing also needs a defined scope. Ask which customer tasks, access rules, devices, and failure cases will be checked. If the product handles sensitive information, identify any specialist review it needs early enough to include the work.

If AI is part of the product, discuss how its outputs will be checked and what happens when they are unsuitable. That is a different cost question from whether the developer uses AI tools while writing code.

### Deadlines and Review Decisions

A deadline changes the planning constraints, but it does not establish how much work can fit before it. Explain why the date matters and ask the developer to identify the scope and dependencies behind the proposed schedule.

Your own decisions can be dependencies. If wording, designs, account access, or business rules need your approval, agree when you will provide it. Ask how delayed decisions affect the plan and whether they can create additional cost.

Treat new requests explicitly too. A change to a business rule can affect several parts of the product even when the interface looks almost identical.

## What Should an MVP Estimate Include?

Before comparing two proposals, check that they describe comparable deliverables and responsibilities. The following questions help you find work that may be included in one total but left for you to arrange in another.

| Part of the Estimate | What to Confirm |
| --- | --- |
| Deliverables and exclusions | What will be usable at the end, and what is outside the agreement? |
| Design and supplied assets | Who prepares the layouts, wording, images, and necessary interface states? |
| Connections and data | Which systems and records are included, and who provides access or cleans the source data? |
| Completion checks | What behavior must work before you accept the delivery, and who checks it? |
| Release work | Does the estimate include putting the product online, configuring accounts, and checking the live version? |
| Reviews and changes | What review work is included, and how will additional requests be assessed? |
| Support | What help is included after release, for how long, and under what conditions? |

Keep the assumptions attached to the amount. “Existing records will be supplied in the agreed format” is useful information if someone has to prepare those records before the build can proceed.

Also agree how to distinguish a defect from a change. If the delivered software fails an agreed completion check, ask how correction is handled. If you request new behavior after approving the scope, ask for its effect on the budget before authorizing the work.

The payment arrangement affects how these decisions are charged. Whatever arrangement you choose, a headline total needs enough detail for you to understand what you are committing to.

## Which Costs Continue After Launch?

Once the product is available, your spending changes from preparing a release to keeping it usable and learning from it. Separate these continuing commitments so you can see which charges depend on time, usage, or a new decision.

1. **Subscriptions and infrastructure:** Hosting, databases, storage, domains, and other services may have recurring charges. Record billing periods and renewal dates.
2. **Usage charges:** Messages, transactions, file transfers, and AI requests can have charges linked to activity. Ask which measures affect the bill and what usage the estimate assumes.
3. **Maintenance and support:** Someone needs to handle reported problems, relevant software updates, and operational checks. Agree the responsibility and what paid support covers.
4. **Product revisions:** Changes prompted by user feedback need their own allowance. They may be worthwhile even when the original delivery works as agreed.
5. **Manual operations:** A process handled by staff still consumes time. Include paid help where needed, and record work you will do yourself even when it creates no immediate invoice.

Ask the developer to show the assumptions behind service estimates. For example, [AWS Pricing Calculator](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pricing-calculator/latest/userguide/what-is-pricing-calculator.html) lets you review estimates for selected service configurations. AWS explains that its calculation depends on the information entered. An estimate made for a small trial therefore needs review if expected activity changes.

Check spending controls as well as starting prices. [Supabase's cost-control documentation](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/cost-control) explains that its Spend Cap covers certain usage items, leaves others outside it, and can restrict further usage when covered quotas are exceeded. Ask what a spending limit would mean for your customers' ability to use the product.

You may also need money for recruiting trial users, preparing a marketing site, or other business work. Keep those lines visible in your overall plan without assuming they are part of the software agreement.

## Build an MVP Budget You Can Review

Bring the estimate and outside commitments into one record before deciding whether the first version is affordable. Use the following worksheet fields for each cost item so you can trace an amount back to its source and assumptions.

| Budget Field | What to Record |
| --- | --- |
| Item | The work, service, or responsibility you are budgeting for |
| Included in the quote? | Included, separately charged, or still to be confirmed |
| Amount and currency | The supplied amount or range, with its source and date |
| Billing basis | One-time, subscription, or usage-based, including the relevant unit |
| Payment timing | Deposit, milestone, monthly bill, renewal, or other due date |
| Responsible person | Who pays, approves the charge, or performs the work |
| Assumptions and unknowns | What the amount depends on and what remains unresolved |
| Review point | When or under what condition you will revisit it |

Start with the agreed build work, then add separately paid setup, ongoing services, support, and intended revisions. If hosting is included for an initial period, record when that arrangement ends instead of counting the same charge twice.

Choose a planning period that covers the release and the trial you intend to run. Add the payments due during that period, including renewals or deposits. This helps you distinguish a project's total commitment from the cash you need at a particular stage.

Leave unknown amounts marked “to confirm.” A blank or unknown cost is not zero. Identify who will obtain the missing information before you rely on the total.

Keep a reserve for unresolved risks separate from money allocated to planned improvements. Ask which uncertainties could change the estimate and whether a bounded investigation could reduce them. There is no single reserve percentage that can replace that discussion.

## How to Reduce MVP Cost Without Losing the Core Task

If the budget is too high, ask the developer to price a smaller workable alternative. Compare the whole consequence of each change, including the operating responsibility it creates, before choosing the lowest build total.

Useful options to assess include:

- **Serve a narrower context:** Support the user group or device that lets you run the intended trial. Confirm that the people you need to learn from can still complete the task.
- **Adapt an existing tool:** Compare configuration, subscription, integration, and data-export needs with custom implementation.
- **Limit automation:** Where a person can responsibly handle part of the task, agree their capacity and response time. Review when that workload would become unaffordable.
- **Stage a later capability:** Ask what preparation it genuinely needs now and what can wait until there is evidence to justify the spending.

Compare these alternatives against the same outcome and completion checks. Removing the only way to recover a failed submission may lower the estimate while leaving the first version unable to do its job.

For an AI-assisted build, ask what work the proposed estimate includes for review, testing, and release. The use of a coding tool by itself does not tell you the cost of delivering the agreed product.

## What to Prepare Before Asking for an Estimate

You do not need to write a technical specification alone. Give the developer enough context to identify the work, explain the open questions, and discuss a useful first version within your available resources.

Prepare a short description covering:

- **The user and task:** Who will use the first version and what they need to complete.
- **The proposed boundary:** What you want included and what you expect to leave for later.
- **Existing assets:** Designs, code, documents, software accounts, and records available for review.
- **Required connections:** Outside systems the product needs to use and whether access is available.
- **Constraints:** Important devices, data-handling needs, dates, and known restrictions.
- **Available resources:** Your budget, time for reviews, and capacity to handle manual work.
- **Open questions:** Decisions or technical assumptions that still need investigation.

Be clear about the budget limit as well as the desired outcome. It gives the developer a basis for discussing what can be delivered, what needs further investigation, and whether a different first step would be more useful.

## Final Thoughts

A useful MVP budget lets you make a decision about a specific first version. It should be clear enough to show whether you can fund the release and continue the trial long enough to learn from it.

If you would like to discuss your MVP, bring the task you want users to complete, the assets you already have, and the questions you have not resolved. Those details give us a concrete starting point for talking about the work and its cost.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Two practical details can still affect what you pay even after the work has been described. Clarify the treatment of invoice charges and the validity of the estimate before using its amount to make a commitment.

### Should Taxes and Currency Conversion Be Included in My MVP Budget?

**Yes. Include any applicable taxes, payment fees, and currency-conversion charges you will pay in your MVP budget.** Confirm whether they are already included in the quote so you do not count them twice, and agree on the invoice currency and who pays transfer fees.

If you pay in a different currency, the amount leaving your account can change before the invoice is paid. Record the original quoted amount, the conversion rate used for planning, and any conversion fees so you can review the total when payment is due.

### How Long Is an MVP Estimate Valid?

**An MVP estimate is valid for the period stated by the developer, provided its scope and assumptions still apply.** There is no standard expiry period for every project. Check the estimate's validity or review date and the scope version before using the figure to commit to the work.

If no validity period is stated, get written confirmation that the amount still applies before accepting it. Ask for an updated estimate when the scope, planned start date, supplier prices, required access, or other assumptions change.

title: MVP Feature Prioritization: Which Features Belong in Your First MVP?
excerpt: This guide explains MVP feature prioritization through a worked example and a worksheet. You'll learn how to assess requests, discuss dependencies with a developer, assign manual work, and decide what belongs in your first release.
body:
> **At a glance**
>
> This guide explains MVP feature prioritization through a worked example and a worksheet. You'll learn how to assess requests, discuss dependencies with a developer, assign manual work, and decide what belongs in your first release.

MVP feature prioritization is deciding which features your first release needs, which can be handled another way, and which can wait. The starting point is the useful task a customer needs to finish.

Your list might contain a request form, a reporting dashboard, automatic messages, payments, and a mobile app. To decide which belong in the first release, start with the purpose of that release.

A minimum viable product, or MVP, helps you test an important assumption before investing further. So when deciding how to prioritize MVP features, ask what users must be able to do and what you need to learn from their use.

## Step-by-Step MVP Feature Prioritization

This MVP feature prioritization framework turns each proposed feature into a decision you can review with a developer. Work through the steps in order, recording an investigation when you need more information before committing to an approach.

### 1. Define the First Task and What You Need to Learn

Before choosing features, write down who the first version serves, what they need to do, and what counts as a useful result. Use that description to judge each request and explain why it belongs in the first release.

To help you apply these questions to your own product, we'll follow one example through the article. You'll see how to turn a customer task into feature decisions you can discuss with a developer. The example is an imaginary community workshop that lends tools to its members. It is a planning example, not a client project.

Suppose members currently contact a coordinator to ask about borrowing a tool. The proposed service lets them view the tools, request borrowing dates, and receive a confirmed or declined request. The coordinator checks availability and records when a tool is collected and returned.

For this example, the first trial serves existing members under the workshop's current lending rules. The software does not collect payments or deposits.

The question to explore could be whether members can submit enough information for the coordinator to resolve requests without repeated clarification. During the trial, the workshop would record incomplete requests, follow-up messages, and the help people need. Records from the current process could provide a useful comparison.

For this trial, the proposed service promises coordinator-reviewed requests. Members would be told when to expect a decision.

Write your own starting point in a few sentences:

- Who will use the first version?
- What do they do today?
- Where does their task start, and what result finishes it?
- What do you need to learn from their use?

Keep the learning question specific. Completing requests would tell the workshop something about the process. It would not establish that other workshops would pay for the software.

### 2. Find the Need Behind Each Feature Request

A request usually names a solution. Ask what the person needs to achieve before deciding to build it. The same need may have several workable solutions, with different costs, effort, and responsibilities.

The UK government's Government Digital Service (GDS) makes this distinction in its [guidance on understanding user needs](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/start-by-learning-user-needs): describe the user's problem and ground it in research. That principle is useful when planning a small business product too.

For the workshop, the conversation might look like this:

| Requested feature | Possible underlying need | Question to explore |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Push notifications | Members need to know whether their request was accepted | Would a message through an existing channel reach them? |
| Live availability calendar | Members need a tool for particular dates | Can they wait for coordinator confirmation, or do they need an immediate answer? |
| Reports dashboard | The coordinator needs to see unresolved requests and outstanding tools | Would a simple working list provide the information? |

These are possible explanations to check with users.

Ask about the last time the problem happened. What was the person trying to do? What information was missing? How did they work around it?

Record the difference between an observation and a suggestion. A member asking for notifications tells you they requested notifications. You still need to understand what they are missing and which approach would help.

Group requests that address the same need before evaluating them. This lets you compare alternative approaches without treating each suggestion as a separate commitment.

### 3. Ask What Happens If You Leave a Feature Out

For each proposed item, describe the consequence of removing it. Connect the decision to the task, the people using the service, and what you need to learn. A feature may belong in the first release because it:

- Lets someone complete a necessary part of the task.
- Supports appropriate access, accurate information, or reliable operation.
- Provides evidence needed for the trial's learning question.

If none of those reasons applies, consider postponing it. If one does apply, check whether a smaller feature, an existing tool, or a manual process can meet the need.

#### MVP Feature List: An Example First Release

The following MVP feature list applies the inclusion test to the imaginary workshop. Each row records a delivery decision and its reason, so a developer can review the proposed scope and its assumptions.

| Item | Initial decision | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tool information and a request form | Build now | Members need to identify a suitable tool and submit the required details. |
| A saved request and clear submission status | Build now | Members and staff need to know whether the request was received. |
| A coordinator list with request decisions and loan records | Build now | Staff need to manage the work and record collection and return. |
| Availability checks and messages to members | Handle manually | The coordinator may be able to use the current records and an existing communication channel. |
| A connection to the existing stock system | Investigate first | Access, record accuracy, and update behavior are unknown. |
| An instant availability calendar | Postpone conditionally | Coordinator review may be sufficient, provided members can accept the delay. |
| Automatic reminders and a reporting dashboard | Postpone | Manual follow-up and a simple operational list may cover the trial. |

These decisions depend on the service being offered. If the workshop needs a deposit before confirming a loan, that requirement changes the plan.

Also distinguish a reporting dashboard from the screen staff need to do their work. A coordinator who cannot find pending requests cannot run this service. The operational view needs to be included in the scope.

Agree on what correct behavior looks like. For this example:

- Members see only the request information they are allowed to access.
- Authorized staff can record decisions and loan status.
- A request marked as saved remains available when reopened.
- A failed submission clearly tells the member that the request has not been received.
- Retrying an action does not leave staff with confusing duplicate records.

These are starting points for a discussion with the developer. They need to determine how to implement and verify the behavior.

### 4. Check Dependencies and Unknowns With Your Developer

A dependency is something a feature needs before it can work. Recording the coordinator's decision depends on having a saved request, identifying the correct member, and controlling who can change the record. That supporting work can be essential even if members never see it.

Ask the developer to look at the complete task. Estimating a screen without its supporting behavior can leave important work out of the discussion.

Consider the proposed stock-system connection. A live availability display might need answers to questions such as:

- Can the software access the existing records?
- Do those records distinguish each tool clearly?
- How are collection, return, and unavailable tools recorded?
- How quickly do changes appear?
- What happens if two requests overlap or the connection fails?

You do not need to answer the engineering questions yourself. You need to make the uncertainty visible before treating the feature as agreed work.

An investigation could be recorded like this:

**Question:** Can the current stock records support the availability information the service needs?

**Owner:** The developer, working with the person who maintains those records.

**Evidence to return:** Available access, sample records, update limitations, unresolved problems, and implications for the build.

**Next decision:** Use a workable manual check, approve a connection with a reviewed scope, or change the proposed service.

Agree on the extent of that investigation before it begins. It should return information that helps you make a decision.

Ask for effort estimates that include relevant design, development, testing, setup, and continuing responsibilities. Keep the unknowns attached to the estimate. An untested connection should not receive a confident estimate merely to complete a spreadsheet.

If all the necessary work exceeds your available time or budget, revisit the audience, task, or approach. Removing a required safeguard or a prerequisite can leave you with a release that cannot do its job.

### 5. Give Manual Work an Owner and a Limit

Manual delivery creates operating work every time someone uses the service. Compare that continuing workload with the effort of building and maintaining automation before deciding what the trial can support.

For the workshop's manual availability checks and follow-up, agree:

- Who checks requests and who covers their absence.
- When members should expect a response.
- How staff avoid confirming conflicting loans.
- Where decisions and follow-up work are recorded.
- What signs would show that the workload is becoming unmanageable.

“Someone can email them” leaves these responsibilities unresolved.

Also check whether existing software already covers part of the task. You may be able to use the workshop's current messaging and records tools, provided access is appropriate and the process stays consistent. Compare that work with maintaining a new feature.

Keep the test aligned with the promise. Coordinator review can help test the usefulness of an online request process, but it cannot establish that an automated availability system works. If members need immediate confirmation, investigate that requirement before relying on manual review.

### 6. Complete a Feature Decision Worksheet

Use a short record for each substantial feature. Split a broad item when its parts serve different needs or have different priorities. Start the document with your first audience, complete task, and learning question. Then work through these fields:

| Question | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| What has been requested? | The proposed behavior in plain language. |
| Who needs what result? | The need behind the request and its place in the task. |
| What evidence do we have? | Observations, requests, existing records, or business rules. Mark assumptions clearly. |
| What happens without it? | The specific problem caused by leaving it out. |
| Is there another workable approach? | A smaller feature, existing tool, or manual process. |
| What does it depend on? | Required data, access, other features, or connected systems. |
| What effort and uncertainty are involved? | Developer input, including checks, setup, and continuing work. |
| What will we do? | Build now, use an existing tool, handle manually, investigate first, or postpone. |
| Who owns the next action? | The person responsible and any review or response expectations. |
| What could change the decision? | Evidence to gather and a point at which to review it. |

For example, a record for automatic reminders might say:

> **Need:** Staff need to follow up when tools have not been returned.
>
> **Current knowledge:** This is part of the imaginary workshop's lending process. We have no trial evidence yet showing how much follow-up the proposed service would create.
>
> **Alternative:** The coordinator checks outstanding loans and contacts members through the agreed channel.
>
> **Decision:** Postpone automatic reminders while assigning manual follow-up to the coordinator.
>
> **Dependency:** Any later reminder feature needs accurate return dates, loan status, and suitable contact details.
>
> **Reconsider when:** Missed returns persist despite the agreed process, or follow-up becomes more work than staff can manage.

After reviewing individual items, walk through the whole task again. Check that the included work forms a complete service and that required dependencies have been covered.

### 7. Choose a Method for Comparing the Remaining Options

A framework can help you compare the choices left after completing the worksheet. Choose one that fits the evidence you have and the decision you need to make, rather than applying several methods to the same list.

| Approach | Useful question | What you need first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Value versus effort | Which workable option contributes more for the effort involved? | A specific outcome and developer input on effort. Easy work still needs a reason to belong. |
| MoSCoW | Which requirements are commitments for this release? | An agreed release boundary and a reason for each priority. |
| RICE | How do several opportunities compare using a consistent score? | Supported estimates of reach, impact, confidence, and effort. |

#### MoSCoW: Agree What Matters in This Release

The [Agile Business Consortium's MoSCoW guidance](https://www.agilebusiness.org/resource/what-is-moscow-prioritization/) defines four priority groups for an agreed delivery period. Use them to explain the importance of each requirement and set expectations about what the release will include:

- **Must have:** The release cannot deliver a viable outcome without it.
- **Should have:** Important, but the release remains workable without it.
- **Could have:** Useful, with less consequence if it is left out.
- **Won't have this time:** Explicitly outside the current release.

Use the consequences of omission recorded in your worksheet to assign each group. An acceptable workaround can change whether a particular implementation is a must-have.

Keep the distinction between priority and delivery approach. MoSCoW describes importance within a release. Your worksheet also records whether the need will be met through custom software, an existing tool, or manual work.

#### RICE: Use Scores When You Can Support the Inputs

RICE compares reach, impact, confidence, and effort. Reach concerns how many people or events an option affects within a defined period. Confidence reflects the support behind your estimates.

[Intercom's original explanation of RICE](https://www.intercom.com/blog/rice-simple-prioritization-for-product-managers) recommends using real measurements where possible and including work across the team in effort. It also explains why dependencies can justify doing work outside score order.

If you cannot support the inputs yet, keep the assumptions visible and use a qualitative discussion while gathering evidence. Calculating a score does not supply the missing information.

### 8. Resolve Competing Requests Before Changing the Scope

Suppose the coordinator asks for a loan-extension screen while members ask to choose a collection time online. Both requests affect borrowing, but they solve different problems and need separate evidence.

For each request, identify who is being blocked, what happens now, and whether the problem affects the promised task. An occasional preference and a recurring inability to collect a tool deserve different attention.

Ask the developer about the consequences too. Extending a loan changes the expected return date. Offering collection times may require opening hours and limits on how many people staff can serve. Those rules need agreement before the screen can be estimated.

If both changes are necessary and do not fit, revisit the release scope, time, or budget. Choosing the easier screen alone does not resolve the other requirement.

When you accept a change, write down:

- What evidence or requirement changed.
- Why the addition belongs in this release.
- What supporting work it needs.
- Whether other work will be removed.
- How it affects the estimate and review date.
- Who approved the decision.

A new idea, a newly discovered requirement, and a fault need different responses. A problem that exposes another member's information or loses requests needs review immediately. A request for a different dashboard layout can be assessed against the current scope.

Agree on the change before the added work starts. This gives both you and the developer a clear record of the decision.

### 9. Give Postponed Features a Reason to Return

A postponed list is useful when it helps you make a later decision. Record what you would need to observe before spending more effort on each item. Avoid treating every entry as a promise for the next release.

For the workshop, record conditions such as these:

| Postponed feature | Evidence that could justify reconsidering it |
| --- | --- |
| Stock-system connection | Re-entering records causes recurring errors or excessive work, and investigation identifies a suitable connection. |
| Reporting dashboard | Staff have a specific recurring decision the operational list and simple trial records cannot support. |

These observations would start another scope discussion. They would not automatically approve development.

Review the reason too. If members struggle to choose the right tool, a live calendar may do little to help. The next improvement might be clearer tool information.

## Final Thoughts

A useful scope discussion starts with your completed worksheet and unresolved questions. Give the developer the sample records and access they need to assess those questions before you commit to the build.

Leave that discussion with one agreed version of the feature list and named owners for any outstanding checks.

## Frequently Asked Questions

When you turn the feature decisions into a development brief, you may still have questions about how to describe the work. These answers clarify feature counts and the need for accounts before you request an estimate.

### How Many Features Should a First MVP Include?

There is no fixed number that defines an MVP. A feature might mean a single button or a complete workflow, so two lists with the same number of entries can represent very different amounts of work.

Use specific descriptions when comparing scope. “Calendar” could mean a date field, a view of requested dates, or a system that checks availability and resolves conflicting bookings. Those are different commitments.

### Does Every MVP Need User Accounts?

Not every MVP needs a full registration and profile system. The decision depends on whether the task requires identifying a person, keeping a record for them, or controlling access to information and actions.

A public calculator that returns a result without storing personal information may not need accounts. A service showing members' private loan records needs an appropriate way to verify who can view or change them. Agree on that access approach with the developer before the trial.

title: How to Build an MVP With One Developer: Plan Your First Useful Version
excerpt: This guide explains how to build an MVP with a developer, from choosing the first useful task to learning from real users. It covers scope, responsibilities, progress reviews, testing, and launch. You'll also find a short planning worksheet to help you agree on what the first version needs to do.
body:
> **At a glance**
>
> This guide explains how to build an MVP with a developer, from choosing the first useful task to learning from real users. It covers scope, responsibilities, progress reviews, testing, and launch. You'll also find a short planning worksheet to help you agree on what the first version needs to do.

You have an idea for a product. Each conversation adds something to it: a dashboard, reminders, payments, perhaps a mobile app. Before long, the feature list is easier to describe than the problem the product should solve.

Before paying for the build, bring the plan back to the first person who will use it. What do they need to finish, and what would make the result useful enough to try?

One developer may be able to build that first version. You still need to make product decisions, provide information, find suitable users, and agree on how you'll judge the result.

## What is a minimum viable product (MVP)?

A minimum viable product, or MVP, is a first version or experiment that helps you test an important assumption about your customers. It gives you a way to see whether people find a result useful before you invest in more of the product. Depending on the question, the first test may involve a service you deliver manually.

This guide focuses on a usable software MVP. People should be able to complete the task you've promised, while you learn whether the result is valuable. The word minimum describes the scope you choose. Accurate records, appropriate access, and a working path to the result are still part of the job.

## How to build an MVP

To build a minimum viable product, choose a customer problem, define a useful task, and decide what the first release needs to test. Then agree how you and the developer will deliver it, check it, and put it into use. The MVP development process below takes you through those decisions and the review that follows the first release.

### 1. Choose one customer problem and one useful result

Start with a specific group of people and a situation they already face. Ask how they handle it today, where the difficulty occurs, and what would make them change their approach. Their existing option might be email, a spreadsheet, another product, or leaving the problem unresolved.

We'll use an imaginary quote approval service throughout this guide. It is a planning example, not a client project.

Suppose a small repair business sends quotes as attachments and follows up by phone. The proposed service lets a customer open a quote on their phone, review the work and price, and approve or decline it. Staff can see the response and arrange the next step.

The useful task ends with a recorded decision. A customer opening a link is only part of that task.

The first question could be whether customers will respond this way with an amount of help the business can manage. That gives you a reason to build and something to observe. Whether repair businesses will pay for the service is another question. Customer use alone won't answer it.

### 2. Choose the MVP scope and essential features

Walk through the task from beginning to end. For the quote service, staff prepare a quote, send it to the intended customer, and receive a recorded response. Sketch the few screens and decisions needed along that path.

Ask whether each proposed feature is necessary to complete the task, run the trial responsibly, or collect the evidence you need. If its purpose is unclear, leave it for a later decision.

| Build for the first release | Handle manually during the trial | Leave for later |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staff can enter and check quote details | Staff prepare the quote and send its link | Accounting and stock-system connections |
| The intended customer can review and respond | Staff answer questions by phone or email | In-app chat and automatic reminders |
| Staff can see the saved response | Staff arrange work after approval | Scheduling and online payments |

Appropriate access and accurate records support the whole task. Customers must see the right quote, and a failed save must not look like a recorded approval. Agree what happens if a quote changes or is withdrawn.

Discuss where people will use the product. A browser-based version may suit this example if customers can complete the task on their phones. A product that depends on particular device capabilities may need a different approach.

Also consider whether existing software or a no-code tool can support the task before choosing a custom build. Check how well that approach fits the required workflow and who needs access to the information.

Manual work also needs an owner. Decide who sends links, handles questions, and follows up. Check how many quotes that person can reasonably manage during the trial.

### 3. Check whether one developer can deliver this scope

Assess the work you have described against the developer's skills and available time. The title full-stack developer usually covers the screens people use and the software and data behind them. It doesn't establish that someone also handles every design, research, security, and support responsibility.

For the quote service, discuss who will design the screens, check access to quotes, prepare the live system, and respond to problems. Some tasks may fit the developer's experience. Others may need a designer or specialist reviewer.

A deadline requiring several pieces of work at the same time, unfamiliar integrations, or demanding security requirements can change the staffing decision. One task can also involve several roles, such as staff and customers, with different permissions.

Your responsibilities matter too. Someone on the business side needs to supply realistic examples, make decisions, review progress, and recruit early users. Agree who covers problems when the developer is unavailable.

### 4. Plan the MVP development process in reviewable stages

Turn the scope into stages with a result you can examine. Y Combinator's [advice on planning an MVP](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/startup-school-week-2-recap-michael-seibel-adora-cheung-and-ilya-volodarsky/) includes writing down what you plan to build. A written scope gives you a reference when new ideas arrive.

For the illustrative quote service, the stages could be:

1. **Agree the first release.** Record the task, sample quote, included behavior, exclusions, access needs, and learning question. Investigate any unknown that could block the task.
2. **Try a complete working version.** On a private test site, follow a quote from staff entry through the customer's response to the staff record. Review the agreed completion checks.
3. **Prepare and run a limited trial.** Finish the required checks, arrange support, invite suitable users, and collect the evidence for your next decision.

Agree target dates, review points, responsibilities, and spending limits for those stages. A delay in sample data, account access, or a business decision can affect the next stage, so record those dependencies.

When a new feature is requested, ask what it changes. You may exchange it for other work, approve additional time and cost, or leave it for later. Record the decision before the added build begins.

Keep the estimate tied to the work. Design, permissions, connected services, existing data, testing, and launch can affect it. Separate the build commitment from hosting, outside services, manual operations, support, and later revisions.

### 5. Test the core task and review working software

Ask for a private test link as working parts become available. Use it to follow the customer's task rather than judging progress only by screenshots.

For the quote service, agree checks such as these:

- The intended customer sees the correct work description and amount.
- Another customer cannot access that quote.
- A response remains saved after the page is reopened and appears for staff.
- A failed save produces a useful message without showing a successful response.
- A changed or withdrawn quote follows the agreed rules.
- The task works on the phones and browsers intended users will have.

Your review and the developer's technical checks have different roles. Ask what they have tested, what remains unresolved, and whether specialist verification is needed. Trying the customer task yourself cannot establish everything about the software underneath.

Also let suitable users attempt the task with little guidance. Watch where they hesitate or misunderstand what will happen. If you explain every action, you may miss a problem with the experience.

Keep three questions separate: does the software behave as agreed, can users complete the task, and do they value the result? A successful technical test answers only part of what you need to know.

### 6. Prepare a small launch you can support

Identify the first users before development finishes. For the quote service, recruit a small repair business willing to try the process with customers who have actual quotes to review. Someone with no current quote has no reason to complete this task.

Agree what the participants will receive, who will answer questions, and how staff will handle the manual work. Explain any limits that affect their use of the service.

Before inviting customers, confirm that the live version passes the agreed checks. Decide who approves the release, who watches for problems, and how to pause or recover if something goes wrong. Check the access, instructions, and backup arrangements needed to operate it, along with ongoing bills and support responsibilities.

Prepare the measurement too. Agree how you'll record quotes sent, customer responses, errors, and requests for help. Keep records focused on the trial's question and discuss what customer information needs to be collected.

### 7. Use the first release to decide what to do next

Choose your measures before the trial begins. The Government Digital Service's [guidance on setting performance measures](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/measuring-success/how-to-set-performance-metrics-for-your-service) connects measures to a service's purpose and recommends combining them with user research. That principle is useful for a small business trial too.

For the quote service, record how many customers received a quote, how many responded through the service, where they needed help, and how much staff effort was involved. An opened link can help explain what happened, but it doesn't establish that the customer completed the task.

Review the evidence over a period that covers normal quote activity. Compare it with the existing process where you have useful records. A small trial can inform a decision without proving that every difference was caused by the software.

Speak with people who used it and those who stopped. If customers want to respond online but struggle with one screen, improve that step. If they see little benefit over a phone call, revisit the approach before adding features. If too few real quotes reached customers, the evidence may be inconclusive.

Agree the next revision and its scope. You might improve the task, investigate willingness to pay, run a better trial, or stop. More features need a reason grounded in what you learned.

### 8. Write down your first-version plan

Bring the decisions together before committing to the main build. You can use this short worksheet with your developer.

| Question | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Who will use the first version? | A specific group and the situation in which they need it |
| What task must they complete? | The starting point, action, and useful result |
| Why would they change their current approach? | The improvement you expect and the assumption you need to test |
| What will the release include? | Essential behavior, intended platform, checks, exclusions, and manual work |
| Who will do the work? | Developer responsibilities, business responsibilities, and any specialist help |
| How will delivery be reviewed? | Stages, completion checks, dependencies, dates, and spending limits |
| Who will use it first? | Suitable participants and the person responsible for support |
| What happens after the trial? | Measures, a review point, and the decisions the evidence should inform |

## Final thoughts

A useful first release gives customers a task they can finish and gives you evidence for the next decision. Its scope should be small enough to manage while covering what people need to reach that result.

Before you commit, write down the task, the work included, who handles it, and what you need to learn. Then agree a first stage you can review with the developer.

If you'd like to discuss your MVP, bring the customer problem, what people do today, and the first useful result you have in mind. Those details give us a concrete starting point for a conversation about the build.

## Frequently asked questions

### How long does it take to build an MVP?

Ask for a schedule against the agreed first release, with time for investigation, development, checks, and your reviews. Make clear which date means the software is ready for a trial and which marks the review of that trial. A product used for occasional tasks may need a longer observation period even after the build is complete. If a fixed date matters, explain why and ask what useful scope can fit it before committing.

### Can I build an MVP without hiring developers?

Yes, for some projects. If existing software or no-code tools cover the task, you may be able to set up and run the first version yourself. You still need to check the workflow, customer access, and saved data, and handle support. If essential behavior is beyond what you can configure and verify, get technical help before putting it into use.

### What makes a successful MVP development process?

A useful process connects the build to a question you need to answer. Agree on the customer task, review working software, check that people can use it, and collect evidence from a real trial. Finish with a decision about what to improve, investigate, or stop. Completing the planned features tells you the build is finished, but you still need to learn whether customers value the result.

### What mistakes should I avoid when building an MVP?

Avoid starting with a growing feature list before you have a clear customer task. Other mistakes include reviewing only screenshots, leaving manual work and support without an owner, and launching without a way to observe real use. Agree on the task, completion checks, responsibilities, and learning question before the main build. These give you a reference when requests or problems arise.

title: Prototype vs MVP: What Should You Build Before Paying for a Full Product?
excerpt: This Prototype vs MVP guide helps you choose what to build before committing to a larger software project. You'll learn what each approach tests, when a technical check or simpler experiment may be enough, and what can carry forward. It also explains what affects the work and what to agree with a developer before paying for the next step.
body:
> **At a glance**
>
> This Prototype vs MVP guide helps you choose what to build before committing to a larger software project. You'll learn what each approach tests, when a technical check or simpler experiment may be enough, and what can carry forward. It also explains what affects the work and what to agree with a developer before paying for the next step.

The prototype vs MVP question comes down to what you need to learn before paying for software development. You might need to see whether people understand a booking process. You might need to check whether your supplier's system will share the data your idea depends on. Or you might need customers to use a small service in their normal work.

Those questions need different tests.

A prototype helps you test a proposed experience. A minimum viable product, or MVP, helps you learn whether an important customer or business assumption holds up. Sometimes a conversation, a manual service, or a focused technical test is the right place to start.

## What is the difference between a prototype and an MVP?

A prototype makes a proposed solution tangible so people can explore and test it. It might be a paper sketch, a set of clickable screens, or something built with code.

For example, someone could try choosing an appointment and changing its date in a prototype. The screens might respond convincingly even though no appointment is saved.

The level of detail should suit the question. In its [guidance on prototype fidelity](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ux-prototype-hi-lo-fidelity/), Nielsen Norman Group describes prototypes that vary in both realism and interactivity, with testing based on watching people attempt tasks.

An MVP serves a learning goal. In his [explanation of an MVP](https://leanstartup.co/resources/articles/what-is-an-mvp/), Eric Ries describes learning about customers with the least effort and makes clear that the right form depends on the context.

That is why people use the term differently. In Lean discussions, an MVP can be a small experiment. In a development proposal, it often means an initial usable product. Ask what the person means before comparing quotes.

For a usable software MVP, people need to complete the task you have promised. Some work behind the scenes may still be manual. A form connected to a service you operate yourself could be enough to test its value. An elaborate automated system may be unnecessary at that point.

These labels can overlap. A prototype used in a customer experiment may contribute to an MVP approach. The useful distinction is what you are testing and what the result will let you decide.

## Prototype vs MVP at a glance

The MVP column below describes a small version that delivers a real outcome to its users. Compare it with a prototype by the question each can answer, the feedback you can collect, and the work that continues afterwards.

| Decision | Prototype | Usable MVP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main question | Can people understand and use this proposed experience? | Will the intended users get value from this version in practice? |
| Who takes part | Intended users, with the founder, designer, or developer observing | Early customers or internal users, plus whoever runs and supports the service |
| What needs to work | Enough of the experience to test the chosen task. Other behavior can be simulated | The promised task must reach a real outcome. Supporting work may be manual |
| Useful feedback | Where people hesitate, misunderstand, or need help | Whether people finish the task, return, pay where relevant, and need support |
| What may carry forward | Findings, content, designs, and code that is suitable for reuse | A working service that may be improved, changed, or replaced |
| Continuing work | Arrange testing, record findings, and revise the idea | Handle the agreed service, user issues, data, fixes, and operating costs |
| Limits of this evidence | A usability session does not establish demand, technical feasibility, or readiness for live use | Early use does not establish long-term demand, profitable operation, or suitability for a much larger audience |

## MVP vs prototype: which should you build first?

Choose the next step by the question you need to answer. Think about what would change your decision to invest further, then choose a test that can provide that evidence. The questions below help you identify a useful starting point.

### Is the problem worth solving?

Start with people who experience the problem. Ask how they handle it now, what goes wrong, and what they have already tried. Then consider a specific offer they can respond to.

A simple page inviting people to request a trial may help you test interest. A manual service may let you test whether the outcome is useful before you automate delivery. These are different experiments within the broader [MVP learning process described by Yevgeniy Brikman](https://www.ybrikman.com/blog/2025/02/10/mvp-is-a-process/).

Keep the conclusion narrow. Someone leaving an email address has agreed to hear more. You still need evidence about use and payment.

### Can people use the proposed solution?

A prototype is useful when the uncertainty concerns the experience. Choose the task you want to observe, such as submitting a request or comparing options. This lets you examine the flow before connecting the systems behind it.

Give intended users a realistic situation and let them try. Record where they need help and what they expect to happen. If you explain every screen as they go, you are learning how well they follow your demonstration.

Before testing, decide which behavior must be realistic and which parts can be left out.

### Can the technology do the essential job?

Ask for a technical proof of concept when an untested capability could prevent the service from working. This is a focused feasibility test. Agree on the capability to test and the evidence that would show it works.

For example, can your application retrieve the required records from a supplier's system? You may need a small working connection and a record of its limits before you need a designed customer portal.

The UK government's Government Digital Service (GDS) gives integration feasibility as an example in its [guidance on testing risky assumptions](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/how-the-alpha-phase-works). The principle is useful here even though the guidance concerns UK public services.

A successful test answers the agreed technical question. It leaves other questions, such as usability and demand, open.

### Will people use the service in practice?

Choose a usable MVP when you need people to complete a real task to learn anything further. Let them finish the promised job in their usual setting, while you observe the result and the help they need.

Define the intended users, the outcome, and what you will observe. Depending on the service, useful evidence might include completed tasks, repeat use, payment, or the amount of help required.

Agree when you will review that evidence and what could make you continue, change direction, or stop. The Lean Startup's [build-measure-learn approach](https://theleanstartup.com/principles) connects building to that next decision.

You do not have to buy a separate prototype project first if the experience is already understood and a usable version is the appropriate test.

## Three situations that make the choice clearer

The following situations are illustrative. They are not accounts of client projects. Each shows how the main unknown changes what is worth building, what evidence you can collect, and which questions will still need a different test.

- **You are planning an unfamiliar booking process:** The main question is whether customers can choose the right service and change an appointment. A prototype could let you observe those tasks before connecting calendars or taking payments. Watch for misunderstandings and needed explanations. Successful clicks would tell you about the flow, while demand would still need testing.

- **Your customer portal depends on a supplier's stock data:** First establish whether you can access the required records with the available permissions. A technical test can check the connection, the data you receive, and important gaps. One successful request would still leave questions about updates, failures, and day-to-day operation.

- **You want to sell a reporting service to small businesses:** You could prepare an initial report manually and see whether it helps with a real decision. Agree what is being offered and whether it is paid. Observe whether customers request another report and how much work delivery takes. If the next question requires customers to use a service themselves, a small software MVP may be appropriate. A useful manual report would still leave the cost and feasibility of automation to investigate.

The next step follows the uncertainty. It does not have to follow the same sequence in every project.

## Can the prototype become the MVP?

Some of the work may carry forward. Useful findings, clearer wording, tested layouts, and agreed workflows can all inform development. That does not mean the underlying code is ready for customers.

Code needs a separate assessment. A convincing prototype might use sample data or skip access controls, error handling, and other work needed for live use. In its [guidance on coded prototypes](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/making-prototypes), GDS explicitly cautions against copying prototype code straight into production.

Ask the developer to explain what can be kept, what needs changing, and why. A demonstration alone does not tell you how much development remains.

The same judgment applies after an MVP. If the initial version serves its users and is suitable to maintain, it can evolve. If the evidence points to a different approach, some work may need replacing. Calling something an MVP does not decide that question in advance.

## What changes the time and investment?

Ask for an estimate against a defined test. The label alone tells you very little about the work. Before comparing proposals, check the scope of the experiment, the work needed to run it, and the responsibilities that continue afterwards.

- **Scope and research:** A prototype covering one decision is a different assignment from a realistic simulation of several user journeys. Research also takes effort. Someone needs to find suitable participants, prepare tasks, observe sessions, and interpret the findings.

- **Connections and technical unknowns:** For a usable service, discuss the systems it connects to, the data it handles, the people who can access it, and the help users may need. Unfamiliar technology and unclear requirements can create additional investigation and revisions.

- **Work after delivery:** Hosting, outside services, manual operations, support, and further changes may continue for as long as the service runs.

Compare proposals using their scope, assumptions, and deliverables. Universal price ranges or fixed build times cannot tell you what your particular test requires.

## What to agree before you pay for the next step

A short written agreement should make these points clear. Use them to make sure you and the developer expect the same result, understand the limits of the work, and know how you will decide what happens next.

- **The question:** What do you need to learn before spending further?
- **The participants:** Who will test or use it, and how will you reach them?
- **The deliverable:** Will you receive screens, working code, a technical result, or a usable service?
- **The limits:** What is real, what is simulated, and what is outside the scope?
- **The evidence:** What will you observe, and how will you record it?
- **The next decision:** When will you review the result, and what would justify continuing, changing, or stopping?
- **The handover:** What will you own or have access to, what may be reused, and who handles ongoing work and costs?

If you want help choosing that first step, bring the problem, what you already know, and the question that would change your decision. That gives a developer something concrete to assess before you commit to a larger build.
